Field surveys of Macrobrachium vollenhovenii in West African river systems have provided detailed measurements of population structure and life-history transitions. Analysis of length-frequency data from the Cross River estuary revealed that individuals recruit to the benthic population at a mean length of 2.45 centimeters , while the largest individuals sampled attain an ultimate total length of 14.45 centimeters [Li = 14.45 centimeters]. Size at puberty, determined from the length frequency of ovigerous females collected during the peak breeding month of August, was estimated at 8.45 centimeters [Lp = 8.45 centimeters]. This intermediate threshold marks the onset of reproductive capability and aligns with the species' position as one of the larger members of the genus within African freshwaters.

The wet weight at birth for Macrobrachium vollenhovenii, derived from morphometric data on egg dimensions typical of palaemonid embryos, is approximately 0.000085 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000085 grams]. This minute neonatal mass reflects the species' high fecundity and the substantial metabolic investment in producing a large number of small offspring. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult body mass, was calculated using length-weight relationships standardized against the congeneric Palaemon elegans, yielding a value of 42 grams [Wwi = 42 grams]. The mass at puberty, similarly inferred from relative weight at sexual maturation, was estimated at 10.25 grams [Wwp = 10.25 grams]. This transition point, representing roughly one-quarter of the final adult mass, indicates that individuals begin allocating resources toward gonadal development well before they have completed somatic growth, a reproductive strategy common among caridean shrimps.

Reproductive output in Macrobrachium vollenhovenii is substantial and tightly coupled to water temperature. At a stable thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], field data indicate that a single female can produce approximately 137 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 137 eggs per day] during peak reproductive activity. This high daily fecundity, sustained over several months, translates into a very large total annual reproductive investment. Egg-bearing females were observed throughout the year from June to December, with a pronounced peak in August, suggesting that the breeding season is timed to coincide with the warmer, wetter period when larval food resources are most abundant and stable water levels facilitate juvenile dispersal.

At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the age at recruitment, defined as the transition from a planktonic larva to a benthic juvenile, was established at 45 days . This 45-day period encompasses the entire larval development phase, from hatching through several zoeal stages to the metamorphic molt into a post-larval shrimp, after which the young prawns settle into the riverbed substrate. The consistency of this developmental timeline, measured under the warm 28 °C conditions typical of the dry season, is critical for synchronizing recruitment with favorable environmental conditions. Survival during this planktonic phase is likely influenced by predation pressure, food availability, and the maintenance of stable salinity gradients in estuarine nursery habitats.

Longevity and the timing of first reproduction in this species are closely linked to thermal conditions. The maximum lifespan for Macrobrachium vollenhovenii, based on field estimates from mark-recapture studies and growth increment analysis, is 912 days [am = 912 days] at a habitat temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly 2.5 years, is typical of medium-sized caridean shrimps in tropical systems. First reproduction, as indicated by the earliest observation of egg-bearing females following the recruitment pulse, occurs at 270 days after the post-larval stage [tR = 270 days after the post-larval stage] under the same warm thermal regime of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. This 9-month interval between settlement and first spawning reflects the time required for juveniles to grow through the size classes, accumulate sufficient energy reserves, and undergo the hormonal changes necessary for ovarian maturation.
